eligibility_reason: HERO converts dialogue history into a heterogeneous memory graph (Episodic Traces, Episodic Units, Episodic Cues, Profile Insights/Cues) written incrementally at run time as new dialogues arrive, and later queried by the agent to condition its answers on prior turns/sessions: 'HERO supports incremental updates: new dialogues create local nodes and edges (linking to the latest predecessor and merging new cues), without full graph reconstruction' (p. 4), and retrieval proceeds via a three-phase cue-activation/graph-traversal process over that same graph (p. 4). Published 2026 (arXiv, p. 1), English, full 15-page paper (extraction note), no exclusion criterion applies: it is not a hardware/cache paper (not E1), the store is externalized and agent-written, not purely parametric (not E2), the agent writes into the graph rather than only reading a fixed corpus (not E3), it is a primary method paper, not a survey (not E4), memory is the entire contribution, not incidental (not E5), and the system is explicitly framed as agent memory for long-horizon interactions (not E6).

facets.justification: The contribution list (p. 2) states 'We design a heterogeneous memory graph that preserves complete dialogue episodes as final evidence.' Page 4 describes nodes (Episodic Traces, Episodic Units, Episodic Cues, Profile Insights) and edges built via 'structural inclusion, semantic indexing, and temporal chaining,' with Table 8 (p. 12) reporting per-user node/edge counts, confirming the memory is stored and traversed as a graph the agent writes to.

The paper's contribution is framed explicitly against prior compression/rewriting approaches: the abstract and p. 2 contributions state HERO 'preserves raw dialogue text as evidence for reasoning, thereby mitigating information loss' rather than rewriting or replacing memories, and p. 4 states the Episodic Layer supports 'variable-resolution retrieval from coarse traces to fine-grained facts without irreversible compression,' with incremental updates that 'create local nodes and edges... without full graph reconstruction.' Profile Insights are described as guidance signals derived from traces, but p. 2 is explicit that 'these profile nodes act as navigational bridges rather than replacement memories' — the primary evidence store (Episodic Traces) is appended, not rewritten.

Page 4 declares a three-phase, explicitly combined retrieval procedure: '(1) Initial Anchor Identification' via embedding cosine-similarity thresholding against cue nodes, '(2) Iterative Context Expansion' via cue-context-cue graph traversal, and '(3) Global Relevance Propagation and Evidence Ranking' using 'Personalized PageRank initialization' (also described in the Figure 1 caption on p. 4) that combines activated Episodic-Unit and Profile-Insight cues. This is a stated fusion of similarity matching, graph traversal, and rank propagation, not a single unranked mechanism.

Evidence is drawn entirely from lab-style comparison: Table 6 (p. 12) compares HERO against baselines (MemoryOS, Mem0, MemU, MemOS, Zep, EverMemOS) on LoCoMo, ablations against HERO variants appear in Figure 2 (p. 8), and hyperparameter sensitivity is reported in Table 5 (p. 8) and Table 7 (p. 12) on the LoCoMo and PERSONAMEM benchmarks. No real users, deployment, or fielded system is reported in any given page; the Conclusion (p. 8) frames the results as validating the framework on benchmark datasets, not in a live setting.

The paper reports scores against baselines on two fixed benchmark datasets — LoCoMo (56.06% F1, per p. 2 contributions) and PERSONAMEM (70.63% accuracy) — with per-backbone comparison tables (Table 6, p. 12) and top-k sensitivity tables (Table 7, p. 12); this is a benchmark-suite comparison rather than a manipulated controlled-experiment condition or a bare proof-of-concept run.

The paper repeatedly self-identifies HERO as a 'framework' organizing two integrated components — graph-based memory construction and profile-guided retrieval — rather than a single algorithm: the title and abstract name it 'Human-profile Enhanced Retrieval Optimization framework for long-term agent memory,' and the contributions on p. 2 list both a construction design ('a heterogeneous memory graph') and a separate retrieval-mechanism design as parts of one architecture, with no released artifact/tool described in the given pages that would make 'tool' the better fit.
